message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) belong to very different branches of the mammalian tree:

| Taxon | Order | Super‑order | Key traits |
|-------|-------|-------------|------------|
| Lion | Carnivora | Laurasiatheria | Carnivorous, feliform |
| Zebra | Perissodactyla | Laurasiatheria | Odd‑toed ungulate, herbivorous |

Because both orders are part of the same super‑order **Laurasiatheria**, their most recent common ancestor (MRCA) is the MRCA of that super‑order.  
That ancestor was a small, probably insect‑eating mammal that lived roughly **70–80 million years ago** during the Late Cretaceous, after the split of Laurasiatheria from other placental mammals but before the divergence of the lineages that would become Carnivora (including Felidae) and Perissodactyla (including Equidae).

So, the common ancestor of a lion and a zebra is:

* **A Laurasiatherian mammal that lived ~70–80 Myr ago** – the last common ancestor of the clade that contains both the carnivores and the odd‑toed ungulates.

So their common ancestor would be a more distant mammalian ancestor, perhaps the last common ancestor of all placental mammals (Eutheria). So the last common ancestor of lions and zebras would be the last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria, which is a mammal that lived about 70-80 million years ago. That ancestor would have lived around 70-80 million years ago. But the question might be simpler: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?"
